A wind map taken four metres above the water is useful. But a sail extends across many heights, and the air does not behave identically at all of them. Can we combine those layers into a single picture that better represents the whole sail?

Here, each height contributes according to the combined local chord lengths of the mainsail and jib. The result is a **sail-chord-weighted wind map**.

::: {.callout-note title="What this calculation represents"}
These maps come from an idealised, stationary 3D RANS simulation at a true wind speed of **5 m/s at 10 m**, a true wind angle of **41?**, and a boat speed of **6 knots**. The saved run stopped at iteration 592 and did **not pass all its numerical checks**. Treat the figures as exploratory model results; physical accuracy and mesh independence have not been established.
:::

## One map from many heights

Let $F(x,y,z)$ be a displayed wind-effect value at a given position and height. If $c_m(z)$ and $c_j(z)$ are the mainsail and jib chord lengths, we calculate

$$
\overline{F}(x,y)=
\frac{\int F(x,y,z)\,[c_m(z)+c_j(z)]\,\mathrm{d}z}
     {\int [c_m(z)+c_j(z)]\,\mathrm{d}z}.
$$

A height with more sail chord contributes more. Below a sail?s foot and above its head, that sail contributes nothing. This is a geometric weighting, with no extra weighting for wind speed or aerodynamic load.

For this geometry, the active range is **1.15?11.65 m**. The jib stops contributing at **9.65 m**. The integrated chord areas are 20.202 m? for the mainsail and 12.376 m? for the jib, giving 32.578 m? in total.

## The combined effect

![Estimated change in VMG, averaged over the sail height. Red indicates a worse value and blue a better value relative to the inherited layer references.](combined.svg){#fig-combined fig-alt="Top view of a sailboat and the surrounding chord-weighted VMG effect, with a red-to-blue colour scale."}

[Download the SVG](combined.svg){.figure-download}

The colours use a simple prescribed relationship:

$$
\Delta\mathrm{VMG}=0.18\left(\Delta U_{\mathrm{knots}}-0.18H_{\mathrm{degrees}}\right),
$$

where $H$ is a header: a wind shift that makes the wind come more from ahead on the tack shown. A lift has the opposite sign. This formula is a working approximation, **not a boat polar or a direct prediction of boat speed from the CFD solver**.

Each saved layer already has its own spatial reference. We average these centred values without subtracting a new median afterwards. The combined field and the two contributions retain their existing references; independent centring means their displayed values need not add up exactly.

## Wind speed and wind direction

Using the same weights, we can separate the speed and direction contributions. Both maps express the effect in **knots of estimated VMG**, allowing the same colour scale to be used throughout. They do not display raw wind speed or degrees of wind shift.

![The contribution from changes in wind speed, weighted over the sail height.](speed.svg){#fig-speed fig-alt="Chord-weighted wind speed contribution to estimated VMG around the boat."}

[Download the SVG](speed.svg){.figure-download}

![The contribution from headers and lifts, weighted over the sail height.](direction.svg){#fig-direction fig-alt="Chord-weighted contribution of wind direction changes to estimated VMG around the boat."}

[Download the SVG](direction.svg){.figure-download}

The hull and sail outlines are placement references. The sail outlines are taken at **4 m**, while the colour fields represent the full active height range.

## How the layers are combined

The field is interpolated linearly between saved heights. The integral is split at every saved layer and at each sail?s foot and head. Two-point Gaussian quadrature integrates the product of the linear field and the linear chord exactly within each interval.

If an active part of a vertical column is missing, that location remains masked. Its weight is not reassigned to another height, and missing values are not replaced by zero.

The averaging acts on the scalar wind-effect values before colour mapping. It does not average RGB colours or velocity vectors.

## What this does ? and does not ? tell us

The map helps compare the wind effects across the space around a boat while accounting for how much sail is present at each height. It is **not** an integration of sail pressure or driving force: chord length alone does not describe how strongly each part of a sail is loaded.

For a two-boat study, a separate force calculation at a common boat speed would let us compare the driving forces along the course. Converting that force difference into a speed difference would require a resistance model and further assumptions.

::: {.callout-tip title="A useful distinction"}
A weighted wind map describes the surrounding wind field. A force integral describes the aerodynamic loading on a sail. Both are useful, but they answer different questions.
:::

## Data and provenance

These figures use only the saved **marine_3d_padded_5ms** dataset, also published as the **v1_5ms** result package. No new CFD simulation was run for this article. The figure export reads the scalar layers embedded in the saved standalone 3D wind viewer.

[Figure provenance](provenance.json) records the source file hash and weighting metadata. The original calculation and averaging implementation are in the [Onsdagsbanen repository](https://github.com/chlyhne/Onsdagsbanen/tree/main/cfd).
